Sorting Pattern-Avoiding Permutations via 0-1 Matrices Forbidding Product Patterns<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

We consider the problem of comparison-sorting an _n_-permutation _S_ that _avoids_ some _k_- permutation \(\pi\). Chalermsook, Goswami, Kozma, Mehlhorn, and Saranurak [CGK<sup>+</sup>15b] prove that when _S_ is sorted by inserting the elements into the GreedyFuture [DHI<sup>+</sup>09] binary search tree, the running time is linear in the _extremal function_ \(\mathrm{Ex}(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot),n)\). This is the maximum number of 1s in an \(n\times n0\)-1 matrix avoiding \(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot)\), where \(P_\pi\) is the \(k\times k\) permutation matrix of \(\pi\), and \(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot)\) is the \(2k\times 3k\) Kronecker product of \(P_\pi\) and the "hat" pattern \((\cdot,\cdot)\). The same time bound can be achieved by sorting _S_ with Kozma and Saranurak’s SmoothHeap [KS20].

Applying off-the-shelf results on the extremal functions of 0-1 matrices, it was known that

\(\mathrm{Ex}(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot),n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \Omega(n\alpha(n)), & O\big(n\cdot 2^{(\alpha(n))^{3k/2-O(1)}}\big), \\ \Omega(n\alpha(n)), & O\big(n\cdot 2^{(\alpha(n))^{3k/2-O(1)}}\big), \end{array}\right.\)

where \(\alpha(n)\) is the inverse-Ackermann function. In this paper we give _nearly tight_ upper and lower bounds on the density of \(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot)\)-free matrices in terms of "_n_", and improve the dependence on "_k_" from doubly exponential to singly exponential.

\(\mathrm{Ex}(P_\pi\otimes(\cdot,\cdot),n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \Omega\big(n\cdot 2^{\alpha(n)}\big), & \text{for most}\pi, \\ O\big(n\cdot 2^{O(k^2)+(1+o(1))\alpha(n)}\big), & \text{for all}\pi. \end{array}\right.\)

As a consequence, sorting \(\pi\)-free sequences can be performed in \(O(n2^{(1+o(1))\alpha(n)})\) time. For many corollaries of the dynamic optimality conjecture, the best analysis uses forbidden 0-1 matrix theory. Our analysis may be useful in analyzing other classes of access sequences on binary search trees.

## 1 Introduction

The problem of sorting restricted classes of permutations has been studied for decades. Knuth [Knu73] observed that the class of permutations sortable by a stack is precisely the set of (2,3,1)-avoiding permutations; see [Tar72, BGH<sup>+</sup>10, MSS19, HI01, EG17a, EG17b, FP08, AB15, AMR02] and Bóna’s survey [Bón02] for models of restricted sorting devices. In general, an _n_-permutation _S avoids_ a _k_-permutation \(\pi\) if there do not exist indices \(i_1<\cdots<i_k\) for which

\(\forall p,q\in[k].S(i_p)<S(i_q)\Longleftrightarrow\pi(p)<\pi(q).\)

In this paper we consider the algorithmic problem of comparison-sorting a \(\pi\)-avoiding _S_.

## Decision Tree Complexity.

Fredman \[Fre76\] observed that if _S_ is known to be selected from a permutation set \(\Gamma\), that _S_ can be sorted with \(O(n+log|\Gamma|)\) comparisons. The _Stanley-Wilf conjecture_ (see Bóna \[Bón22\]) states that if \(\Gamma_\pi\) is the set of all \(\pi\)-avoiding permutations, that \(|\Gamma_\pi|\le(c(\pi))^n\), for some constant \(c(\pi)\). This conjecture was reduced to the _Füredi-Hajnal conjecture_ \[FH92\] by Klazar \[Kla00\] and both conjectures were proved by Marcus and Tardos \[MT04\]. Together with Fredman \[Fre76\], this implies that the decision-tree complexity of sorting _S_ is \(O(nlogc(\pi))=O_k(n)\). Subsequent work has attempted to pin down the leading constant \[Kla00, MT04, Cib09, Fox13, CK17\]. Fox \[Fox13\] proved that<sup>1</sup>

\(nlogc(\pi)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
O(kn) & \text{For all}k\text{-permutations}\pi, \\
\Omega(k^{1/2}n) & \text{For some}k\text{-permutation}\pi, \\
\Omega((k/logk)^{1/2}n) & \text{For almost all}k\text{-permutations}\pi.
\end{array}\right.\)

## Algorithmic Complexity.

There are two natural ways to approach the _algorithmic_ complexity of sorting a \(\pi\)-free _S_. The first is to use knowledge of \(\pi\) to structure the sorting process. This approach is sufficient to sort optimally in _O(n_) time when _k_=3 \[Knu73, Art07\], and has had limited success for some patterns with _k_=4. Arthur \[Art07\] gave _O(n_)-time sorting algorithms when \(\pi\in\{(1,2,3,4),(1,2,4,3),(2,1,4,3)\}\), and _O(n_logloglog_n_)-time sorting algorithms when \(\pi\in\{(1,3,2,4),(1,3,4,2),(1,4,2,3),(1,4,3,2)\}\). The _oblivious_ approach to sorting _S_ is to simply use a general-purpose sorting algorithm, but analyze its behavior when _S_ happens to be \(\pi\)-free. This is the approach taken by Chalermsook, Goswami, Kozma, Mehlhorn, and Saranurak \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b\], Kozma and Saranurak \[KS20\], and by our paper. Consider these two general-purpose sorting algorithms:

**BST Sort.** Fix some dynamic binary search tree (BST) algorithm T . Beginning from an empty BST, insert the elements _S_(1)_,...,S(n_) in that order, reorganizing the tree between inserts as T dictates. The number of comparisons is the sum of depths of \((S(i))_{1\le i\le n}\) at the time of their insertion; the _time_ is linear in the number of comparisons and that needed to reorganize the tree via rotations.

**Heap Sort.** Fix some heap data structure H. Insert the elements _S_(1)_,...,S(n_) into the heap in that order, then perform _n_ Delete-Min operations, thereby sorting the sequence.

Chalermsook et al. \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b\] analyzed the performance of BST Sort when T is GreedyFuture \[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\], an online BST that is _O_(1)-competitive with the natural offline Greedy algorithm \[Luc88, Mun00\]. Define _A<sub>S</sub>_ to be the \(n\times n0\)-1 permutation matrix where _A<sub>S</sub>(i,S(i_))=1. If _S_ avoids a _k_-permutation \(\pi\), then _A<sub>S</sub>_ is \(P_\pi\)-free, where \(P_\pi(i,\pi(i))=1\). Define _A_<sub>Greedy(_S_)</sub>(_i,j_)=1 iff the element with rank _j_ is touched by the insertion of _S(i_). Chalermsook et al. \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b\] proved that any occurrence of the "hat" pattern (<u>**?**</u>) in _A_<sub>Greedy(_S_)</sub> contains, within its bounding box, an input point of _A<sub>S</sub>_, and as a consequence, _A_<sub>Greedy(_S_)</sub> avoids \(Q=P_\pi\otimes(\underline{\bullet})\), where \(\otimes\) is the Kronecker product, i.e., each 1 of \(P_\pi\) is replaced by (<u>**?**</u>). (Following convention, 0-1 matrices are<tbc>

\(P_\pi=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\bullet & \bullet \\
\bullet & \bullet
\end{array}\right)Q=P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
\bullet & \bullet & \bullet \\

\end{array}\right)\)

If _X_ is a fixed 0-1 pattern matrix, define Ex(_X,n_) be the maximum number of 1s in an \(n\times n\) matrix that avoids _X_. Thus, the running time of \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b\] can be bounded in terms of Ex(_Q,n_) without knowing exactly what it is.

**Theorem 1.1** (Chalermsook, Goswami, Mehlhorn, Kozma, and Saranurak \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b\])**.** _If S is_ \(\pi\)_-free, BST Sort using_ GreedyFuture _sorts S in O_(Ex(_Q,n_)) _time, where_ \(Q=P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)\).

Observe that _Q_ is a \(2k\times 3k\) _light_ pattern: it contains exactly one 1 per column. There is a well known connection between light patterns and generalized Davenport-Schinzel sequences \[Kla92, FH92, Kes09, Pet11b, Pet15b\]. Applying a simplifying transformation that collapses the first two rows \[FH92, Thm. 2.2\] and then \[Pet15b, Thm. 1.3\], we have the following general upper bound, where \(\alpha(n)\) is the inverse-Ackermann function.

\(\mathrm{Ex}(Q,n)\le\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
2n\alpha(n)+O(n) & k=2 \\
n\cdot 2^{(1+o(1))\alpha^t(n)/t!} & k\text{odd},t=(3k-5)/2 \\
n\cdot(\alpha(n))^{(1+o(1))\alpha^t(n)/t!} & k\text{even},t=(3k-6)/2
\end{array}\right.\) (1)

Thus, by Theorem 1.1, GreedyFuture sorts _S_ in \(O(n\cdot 2^{\alpha(n)^{3k/2-O(1)}})\) time. On the lower bound side, we know that \(\mathrm{Ex}(Q,n)=\Omega(n\alpha(n))\) as every _Q_ contains one of the two patterns shown below, which are associated with order-3 Davenport-Schinzel sequences \[HS86, FH92\].

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\bullet &  \\
\bullet & \bullet
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\bullet &  \\
\bullet & \bullet
\end{array}\right)\)

The Greedy algorithm is theoretically attractive, but cumbersome to implement online as GreedyFuture \[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\]. Kozma and Saranurak \[KS20\] introduced a new heap data structure called a SmoothHeap, and proved Heap Sort with SmoothHeap is _equivalent_ to BST Sort with Greedy. Moreover, SmoothHeap is "naturally" an online algorithm, and is easier to implement than GreedyFuture. One can define an \(n\times n0\)-1 matrix _A_<sub>SmoothHeap(_S_)</sub> in the same way, where _A_<sub>SmoothHeap(_S_)</sub>(_i,j_)=1 iff the _i_th Delete-Min touches the element with rank _j_. It is proved that _A_<sub>SmoothHeap</sub> avoids a matrix equivalent to _Q_.<sup>2</sup>

**Theorem 1.2** (Kozma and Saranurak \[KS20\])**.** _If S is_ \(\pi\)_-free, Heap Sort using_ GreedyFuture _sorts S in O_(Ex(_Q,n_)) _time, where_ \(Q=P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)\).

<sup>2</sup>Strictly speaking the equivalence between Greedy and SmoothHeap swaps the roles of time and space. Sorting _S_ with Greedy is isomorphic to sorting _S<sup>T</sup>_ with SmoothHeap, where _S<sup>T</sup>_ is the transpose permutation: \(S(i)=j\Leftrightarrow S^T(j)=i\). Note that _S<sup>T</sup>_ avoids \(\pi^T\). Since the extremal functions for _Q_ and _Q<sup>T</sup>_ are identical on square matrices, we infer that the time to sort _S<sup>T</sup>_ is also _O_(Ex(_Q,n_)).

The main outstanding question is whether it is possible to sort in _O<sub>k</sub>(n_) time, and in particular, whether the Greedy- or SmoothHeap-based algorithms of \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b, KS20\] already sort in time _O<sub>k</sub>(n_). It would also be interesting to give a non-trivial upper bound on the complexity of BST Sort with a Splay Tree \[ST85\], or Heap Sort with a Pairing Heap \[FSST86\].

## 1.1 New Results

### 1.1.1 Upper Bounds

Our main result is a new upper bound on the extremal function of \(P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)\)-type matrices that has a much weaker dependence on _k_, which immediately gives better upper bounds on the complexity of sorting \(\pi\)-free sequences via \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b, KS20\].

**Theorem 1.3.** _Let_ \(P_\pi\) _be the_ \(k\times k\) _permutation matrix of_ \(\pi\) _and_ \(Q=P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)\) _be a_ \(2k\times 3k\) _light matrix. Then_

\(\mathrm{Ex}(Q,n)\le n\cdot\left(2^{O(k^2)}+O(\alpha(n))^{3k-2}\right)2^{\alpha(n)}=n\cdot 2^{O(k^2)+(1+o(1))\alpha(n)}.\)

**Corollary 1.4.** _If S is_ \(\pi\)_-free, then BST Sort using_ GreedyFuture _and Heap Sort using the_ SmoothHeap _will sort S in_ \(n\cdot 2^{O(k^2)+(1+o(1))\alpha(n)}\) _time._

One can view Corollary 1.4 as improving on the \(n2^{\alpha(n)^{3k/2-O(1)}}\) bound of (1) in two ways. It is an asymptotic improvement in _n_ as it brings the exponent of \(\alpha(n)\) from 3_k/_2-_O_(1) down to 1. However, even if one is tempted to consider \(\alpha(n)\) to be a small constant, it also reduces the dependency on _k_ from _doubly_ exponential to merely _singly_ exponential.

It is possible to improve the factor \(2^{\alpha(n)}\) for a specific product pattern. For example,

**Theorem 1.5.** _If I<sub>k</sub> is the_ \(k\times k\) _identity matrix, then_

\(\mathrm{Ex}(I_k\otimes(\bullet),n)\le 2(k-1)n\alpha(n)+O(kn).\)

### 1.1.2 Lower Bounds

When \(k\ge 2\), all \(Q=P_\pi\otimes(\bullet)\) patterns contain \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{\bullet}\) or its reflection, which is known to have extremal function \(\mathrm{Ex}(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{\bullet},n)=2n\alpha(n)\pm O(n)\) \[HS86, FH92, Niv10, Pet15a\].

We prove that \(\mathrm{Ex}(P_\pi\otimes(\bullet),n)=\Omega(n2^{\alpha(n)})\) whenever \(\pi\) contains (3,1,2) or (2,1,3), or equivalently, when \(P_\pi\) contains \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{\bullet}\cdot\) or \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{\bullet}\cdot\). Thus, Theorem 1.6 implies that the general upper bound of Theorem 1.3 can only be improved in the \(\mathrm{poly}(\alpha(n))\) factor.

**Theorem 1.6.** \(\mathrm{Ex}(W,n)=\Theta(n2^{\alpha(n)})\)_, where_<tbc>

\(W=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
\bullet &  &  \\
 &  &  \\
 &  & \bullet \\
 & \bullet &  \\
 &  & \bullet
\end{array}\right).\)

## 1.2 Pattern-avoidance and the Dynamic Optimality Conjecture

The original _dynamic optimality conjecture_ \[ST85\] states that the (online) Splay BST is _O_(1)- competitive with the optimum offline BST, for any sequence with length \(\Omega(n)\). Today dynamic optimality usually refers to the conjecture that _there exists_ an _O_(1)-competitive BST, with Greedy / GreedyFuture \[Luc88, Mun00, DHI<sup>+</sup>09\] and Splay being the foremost candidates.

It is an open problem to prove _o_(log_n_)-competitiveness for Splay or Greedy, though some _corollaries_ of dynamic optimality have been proved \[ST85, Tar85, Col00, CMSS00, IL16, CGJ<sup>+</sup>23, LT19\]. Many corollaries of dynamic optimality can be characterized by forbidden patterns. For example, the optimum BST executes all of these sequences in linear time.<sup>3</sup>

**Sequential.** The sequential access sequence _S_=(1,2_,...,n_) avoids (2,1).

**Deque.** In a deletion-only deque sequence, _S(i_) is either the minimum or maximum of {_S(i),S(i_+1)_,...,S(n_)}. Deque sequences avoid {(213),(312)}. (In a deque, the accessed elements are also typically deleted from the tree \[Sun92, Pet08\].)

**Preorder and Postorder.** Let _R_ be any BST over {1_,...,n_} and _S_ be a preorder (or postorder) traversal of _R_. Then _S_ avoids (231) (or (312)). (The _Traversal Conjecture_ of Sleator and Tarjan \[ST85\] concerned preorder sequences. If the accessed elements in a preorder sequence are moved to the root and _deleted_, yielding two trees, this corresponds with Lucas’s definition of _Split_-sequences \[Luc91\].)

_k_**-Increasing.** _S_ can be decomposed into (_k_-1) increasing subsequences, or equivalently, _S_ avoids (_k,...,_2,1).

_k_**-Recursively Decomposable.** A permutation _S_ is _k_-recursively decomposable if (i) the 1s of the corresponding permutation matrix _A<sub>S</sub>_ can be partitioned into _k_ non-overlapping rectangles, and (ii) those rectangles are themselves _k_-recursively decomposable, where in the base case, any \(1\times 1\) matrix is _k_-recursively decomposable. These sequences avoid all _simple_ (_k_+1)- permutations.<sup>4</sup>

Figure 1 shows the relationship between the classes of permutations, and  1 gives some known upper bounds on the performance of Splay and Greedy. In particular, our new upper bound on \(\mathrm{Ex}(P_\pi\otimes(\bullet,n)\) improves on the bounds for _k_-recursively decomposable sequences (when preprocessing is not allowed), and _k_-permutation avoiding sequences.

## 1.3 Organization

In Section 2 we review forbidden 0-1 matrix terminology, and some key results. In Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.3, establishing the \(n2^{(1+o(1))\alpha(n)}\) upper bound on \(P\otimes(\bullet,)\)-type matrices. In Section 4 we prove Theorem 4.5’s \(\Omega(n2^{\alpha(n)})\) lower bound on _W_-free matrices. Section 5 presents some additional upper bounds, on \(I_k\otimes(\bullet,)\)-free matrices (Theorem 1.5) and matrices avoiding _W_ and its reflection. We conclude with some open problems in Section 6.

<sup>3</sup>Note that the problem we study in this paper is not on this list. There is no published proof yet to the effect that "accessing a \(\pi\)-avoiding _S_ in \(O_\pi(n)\) time" is a corollary of dynamic optimality. The \(O_\pi(n)\)-height decision-tree implied by Fredman \[Fre76\] is not obviously implementable as a dynamic binary search tree. <sup>4</sup>A (_k_+1)-permutation \(\pi\) is _simple_ if there is no interval \(I\subset\{1,\dots,k+1\}\) with \(|I|\in[2,k]\) such that \(\pi(I)=^\mathrm{def}\{\pi(j)|j\in I\}=I\).

## 2 Preliminaries Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m}\) and \(P\in\{0,1\}^{k\times l}\). The _weight_ of _A_, denoted as \(\|A\|_1\), is the number of 1’s in _A_. We say _P_ is _contained_ in _A_, written _P\ \(\mathrm{Ex}(P,n)=\mathrm{Ex}(P,n,n).\) If _P_ is a \(k\times k\) permutation matrix, it is known that both Ex(_P,n_) and \(\mathrm{Ex}(P\otimes\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{},n)\) are _Ok(n_), but we will be interested in the leading constants as well. **Theorem 2.1** (Marcus and Tardos \[MT04\], Geneson \[Gen09\], Fox \[Fox13\], Cibulka and Kyncl \[CK17\], Geneson \[Gen15\], Geneson and Tian \[GT17\])**.** _Let P be any permutation matrix. Then there exists constants_ \(C_k,C'_k\le 2^{(4+o(1))k}\) _such that_ \(\mathrm{Ex}(P,n,m)\le C_k(n+m),\)
\(\mathrm{Ex}(P\otimes\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\bullet}{},n,m)\le C'_k(n+m).\) ## 3 The Upper Bound ### 3.1 Establishing the General Recurrence Let _P_ be a \(k\times k\) permutation matrix and \(Q=P\otimes(\cdot)\) be the \(2k\times 3k\) forbidden pattern. Define _Qa,b_ to be the \(2k\times(3k-(a+b))\) matrix derived from _Q_ by removing the first _a_ and last _b_ columns. For reasons that will become clear later, we must redefine the _contains_ relation _\<_ differently for the _Qa,b_ matrices. **Definition 3.1.** We will say that _Qa,b\a,b(i,j_)=1 implies _A(ri,cj_)=1 • If \(\forall j\). \(Q_{a,b}(i,j)=0\) then \(\exists j'\). \(A(r_i,j')\neq 0\). In other words, an all-0 row \(Q_{a,b}(i,\cdot)\) cannot match an all-0 row of _A_. (Note that \(j'\) need not be in {_c_1_,...,c_3_k-a-b_}.) Let _A_ be an \(n\times mQ_{a,b}\)-free matrix with weight Ex(_Qa,b,n,m_). We will classify all 1s in _A_ according to the following taxonomy, and bound the number of 1s in each class directly or inductively.

Partition _A_ into _slabs_ of _B_ consecutive columns. A row is called _local_ if it has a non-zero intersection with exactly one slab and _global_ otherwise. The 1s in local/global rows are themselves local/global. Let _ni_ be the number of rows local to slab _i_ and _n_∗ be the number of global rows, so \(n=n^*+\sum_in_i\). Suppose _A(r,c_)=1 is a 1 appearing in a global row _r_ and slab _s_=\[_c/B_\]. We classify this 1 as _first_ if the intersection of row _r_ and slabs 1_,...,s_-1 are zero, _last_ if the intersection of row _r_ and slabs _s_+1_,...,_\[_m/B_\] is zero, and _middle_ otherwise. Since each slab is itself _Qa,b_-free, the total number of local 1s is at most \(\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil m/B\rceil}\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a,b},n_i,m_i),\) (2) where _mi_ is the number of columns in slab _i_, which is exactly _B_ except perhaps the last slab. Similarly, if _A_first and _A_last are the matrices of first 1s and last 1s, then each slab of _A_first is _Q__a,b_+1 free, and each slab of _A_last is _Q__a_+1_,b_-free; see Figure 2. Letting \(n_i^f(n_i^l)\) be the number of rows with first (last) 1s in slab _i_, we can upper bound first and last 1s as follows. \(\|A_\mathrm{first}\|_1+\|A_\mathrm{last}\|_1\le\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil m/B\rceil}\big(\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a,b+1},n_i^f,m_i)+\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a+1,b},n_i^l,m_i)\big)\)
\(\le\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a,b+1},n^*,m-m_{\lceil m/B\rceil})+\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a+1,b},n^*,m-m_1).\) (3) In Eqn. (3) we use the _superadditivity_ of Ex to simplify the expression. For any _R_, \(\mathrm{Ex}(R,n_1,m_1)+\mathrm{Ex}(R,n_2,m_2)\le\mathrm{Ex}(R,n_1+n_2,m_1+m_2)\). Note that \(\sum_in_i^f=\sum_in_i^l=n^*\) and that the first and last slabs contain no last 1s and first 1s, respectively. Let _A_∗ be the \(n^*\times m\) matrix formed by the global rows and containing only the middle 1s. We partition the rows of _A_∗ into horizontal slabs of _G_ rows each, so the intersections of the horizontal and vertical slabs induce \(G\times B\) _blocks_. Call a \(G\times B\) block in _A_∗ _heavy_ if it contains a (\(\unknown\)), and _light_ otherwise. The middle 1s inside heavy/light blocks are themselves called heavy/light. Let _A_heavy and _A_light be the \(n^*\times m\) matrices containing heavy and light 1s, respectively. In a light block, the first 1 and last 1 of each row are called _light-first_ and _light-last_, and all other 1s in the row are _light-middle_. Define \(A_\mathrm{heavy}^\mathrm{c}\) to be the \(n^*/G\times m/B\) matrix obtained by _contracting_ each block in _A_<sub>heavy</sub> to a single entry, i.e., non-zero blocks become 1 and all-zero blocks become 0. Because each heavy block contains a (**.**), \(A_\mathrm{heavy}^\mathrm{c}\) is _P_-free, implying \(\|A_\mathrm{heavy}^\mathrm{c}\|_1\) (the number of heavy blocks) is at most Ex(_P,n_<sup>∗</sup>_/G,m/B_). Since each heavy block consists solely of middle 1s, each is _Q_<sub>_a_+1_,b_+1</sub>-free; see Figure 3. Thus,

\(\|A_\mathrm{heavy}\|_1\le\mathrm{Ex}(P,n^*/G,m/B)\cdot\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a+1,b+1},G,B).\) (4)

Let \(A_\mathrm{light}^\mathrm{c}\) be obtained by contracting the _B_ columns in each slab of _A_<sub>light</sub> to a single column. \(A_\mathrm{light}^\mathrm{c}\) inherits the _Q<sub>a,b</sub>_-freeness of _A_<sub>light</sub> and _A_, so the contribution of light 1s in the light-first and light-last categories is at most

\(2\|A_\mathrm{light}^\mathrm{c}\|_1\le 2\mathrm{Ex}(Q_{a,b},n^*,m/B).\) (5)

If _S_ is a sequence, let |_S_| be its length and ∥_S_∥ the size of its alphabet \(|\Sigma(S)|\). A _block_ is a contiguous sequence of distinct symbols. If _S_ is understood to be partitioned into blocks, \(\unknown S\unknown\) is the number of blocks. Regardless of \(\Sigma(S)\), we can always write _S_ in _canonical form_ over the alphabet {1_,...,_∥_S_∥}, where the symbols are sorted according to their first appearance in _S_. If _S_ is in canonical form, its canonical matrix _AS_ is the \(\unknown S\unknown\times\unknown S\unknown\) symbol-block incidence matrix, i.e., _AS(i,j_)=1 if symbol _i_ appears in block _j_, and 0 otherwise. One cannot quite recover _S_ from _AS_ since _AS_ does not encode the order of symbols within a block. Nonetheless, the transformation is _useful_ inasmuch as subsequences avoided by _S_ often become 0-1 patterns avoided by _AS_. ### Composition and Shuffling. We consider sequences _S_ partitioned into _live_ and _dead_ blocks satisfying extra constraints: • All live blocks have the same length. Dead blocks have variable lengths, and the number of dead blocks between consecutive live blocks is also variable. • The first occurrence of every symbol appears in a dead block, and dead blocks contain only first occurrences. Let \((\unknown S\unknown)\) be the number of live blocks in _S_.

## Composition.

Suppose _U_<sub>top</sub> is a sequence in which all live blocks have length _j_ and _U_<sub>mid</sub> is a sequence with ∥_U_<sub>mid</sub>∥=_j_. The _composition_ \(U_\mathrm{sub}=U_\mathrm{top}\circ U_\mathrm{mid}\) is obtained by replacing each live block _L_ of _U_<sub>top</sub> with a copy _U_<sub>mid</sub>(_L_) over the alphabet of _L_, whereas dead blocks of _U_<sub>top</sub> are inherited by _U_<sub>sub</sub> verbatim. In general _U_<sub>mid</sub>(_L_) can contain both live and dead blocks \[Pet15b\], but in our particular construction _U_<sub>mid</sub>(_L_) contains only live blocks.

## Shuffling.

Now suppose _U_<sub>sub</sub> is a sequence whose live blocks have length _j_ and _U_<sub>bot</sub> is a sequence with (|_U_<sub>bot</sub>|)=_j_. The _left-shuffle_ \(U_\mathrm{sub}\otimes U_\mathrm{bot}\) is obtained as follows. Let \(U_\mathrm{sub}=D_0L_1D_1L_2D_2\cdots L_kD_k\), where _L<sub>i</sub>_ is the _i_th live block, _D<sub>i</sub>_ is zero or more dead blocks, and \(k=(\left|U_\mathrm{sub}\right|)\). Let \(U_\mathrm{bot}^*=U_\mathrm{bot}^{(1)}\cdots U_\mathrm{bot}^{(k)}\) be the concatenation of _k_ copies of _U_<sub>bot</sub> over disjoint alphabets. The _left-shuffle_ is obtained by taking, for all _i_, the block \(L_i=(a_1a_2\cdots a_j)\) and inserting \(a_\ell\), for \(\ell\in[1,j]\), at the _left end_ of the \(\ell\)th live block of \(U_\mathrm{bot}^{(i)}\), then inserting dead blocks _D<sub>i</sub>_ between \(U_\mathrm{bot}^{(i)}\) and \(U_\mathrm{bot}^{(i+1)}\).<sup>5</sup>

## 6 Concluding Remarks

Demaine et al.\[DHI<sup>+</sup>09\] and Pettie \[Pet10\] introduced the idea of representing the behavior of a data structure by a 0-1 matrix in which the axes correspond to _time_ and data structure _elements_. Applying results on forbidden 0-1 matrices in this context is very natural, and has led to sharp or nearly sharp bounds on certain path compression schemes \[Pet10\], structured inputs to binary search trees \[CGK<sup>+</sup>15b, CGK<sup>+</sup>15a, CGJ<sup>+</sup>23, Pet10\], and heaps \[KS20\].

Although the forbidden 0-1 matrix framework is perfectly suited to proving that sorting \(\pi\)-free sequences takes _near-linear_ time, it might be inadequate to establishing an optimal _O<sub>k</sub>(n_) time bound. As we have shown, any \(o(n2^{\alpha(n)})\)-time analysis must use some property _beyond_ \(P_\pi\otimes\left(\bullet\right)\)- freeness. Here it may be useful to consider different ways to decompose a 0-1 matrix; see Guillemot and Marx \[GM14\] and Chalermsook, Gupta, Jiamjitrak, Acosta, Pareek, and Yinghcareonthaworn- chai \[CGJ<sup>+</sup>23\].
